Delivery Forecast for
AC-ME, a SaaS company
A product team of 8 developers · roadmap January to June 2027
11 January 2027
Prepared by Bart Pinnock

Page 1 · for your CEO

What you need to know

AC-ME has promised four dates for the first half of 2027. Checked one at a time, all four look safe. Built in the order the team plans, the first two hold, the third is a coin flip and the fourth is late. The team's pace is steady. There is more work than time, and the last date realistically lands about three weeks late. What is holding the dates back: work waits for a review, work is started out of order, and the customer portal is still growing.

What to change first

  1. Decide which date can move: the mobile app refresh or the reporting dashboard. Both can't hold.
  2. Finish in order. Stop starting work on the mobile refresh and the dashboard until payments has shipped.
  3. Review before starting new work. 7 items are built and waiting for a review today. A waiting review goes before anything new.
  4. Close the scope of the customer portal. It grew by 9 items since December, and every item pushes the two deadlines behind it.

The roadmap, in order

The same team behind every deadline

Look at one deadline at a time and ask: if the team did only this, would it make it? Four times the answer is yes. But the team can't do four things as if each were the only one. This forecast takes the work in the order AC-ME plans to build it, and does not count the team twice.

On its own: the chance if the team worked on nothing else from today. In the roadmap: the chance when it waits for the work before it. Realistic: the date that 85 of 100 runs made.

What I found in the data

What is holding the dates back

  • Work waits for a review. Over the last twelve weeks an item took three weeks from start to done on average. For five of those days it was built and waiting for a review. 7 of the 27 items in progress are waiting today. While an item waits, its developer starts something new. That is how 8 developers came to have 27 items in progress.
  • There is more work than time. The team finished 6 to 12 items a week for twelve weeks, 9 on average. 196 items are left. Twenty weeks at this pace is about 183. The difference lands on whatever comes last.
  • Work is started out of order. 11 of the 27 items in progress belong to the mobile refresh and the dashboard. The forecast assumes the team finishes one thing before starting the next. Work started early there doesn't finish early. It makes payments and the portal later.
  • Six portal items wait on the new payment API. That link is not in the simulation. I found it in the blocker flags. It is another reason to ship payments before anything else.
  • The portal is still growing. 9 items were added since December. The forecast counts the scope as it stands today.

Why

  • The work itself takes about five and a half weeks: 50 items at 9 a week.
  • It can't start until the portal is done, realistically April 1. That leaves four weeks to April 30.

What to do

  1. Nothing in the mobile refresh itself needs fixing. Its date depends on the two before it.
  2. Add nothing ahead of it. Every item added to payments or the portal comes straight off this date. Nine more items ahead of it would take it from 53% to 28%.
  3. Look again at the second run. If the chance is under 40% by then, move the date.

Method

How these numbers were made

The data

Workflow data from Jira Cloud, October 2026 to January 2027: when items moved between statuses, when they were created and resolved, blocker flags. No descriptions, comments or code.

The chance

Each deadline was simulated 10,000 times, with the work before it counted first. Every run draws from the team's own finished work and plays the remaining items forward. The chance is the share of runs that finished by the promised date.

The dates

The realistic date is the one that 85 of 100 runs made, the same measure as in the free Delivery Scan. It is not a guarantee: 15 of 100 runs finished later.

The limits

These numbers are the best case. The simulation counts today's scope, and assumes the team keeps its recent pace and finishes the work in the planned order. It doesn't know which items wait on each other. Where I found that in the data, it is in the findings, in my words. And it can't see what has never happened to this team.

What happens next

On 8 February I run the same numbers again. That second run measures whether the changes worked: whether payments shipped before anything else was started, whether items still wait five days for a review, and whether the scope of the portal stayed closed. You get a short note on what moved and what didn't. If finishing in order turns out to be the hard part, that is a conversation about the Delivery Realign.
